title: Adalimumab: TNF Blockade, Infection Screening, and Injection Safety
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Adalimumab is a TNF inhibitor used for several inflammatory diseases. Before and during therapy, infection risk—including tuberculosis and hepatitis B reactivation—must be taken seriously, and live vaccines are generally avoided while immunosuppressed.
recognize: Fever, cough, weight loss, night sweats, or focal infection symptoms can indicate serious infection.
HBV reactivation can occur in susceptible patients receiving TNF blockade.
priorities: Verify baseline infection/TB/HBV screening status and current infection symptoms.
Hold/escalate suspected serious infection according to the prescribed plan rather than administering reflexively.
assessMonitor: Monitor infection signs, injection reactions, neurologic symptoms, heart-failure worsening, and blood-count/liver abnormalities when ordered.
interventions: Teach correct subcutaneous injection, storage, site rotation, and sharps disposal.
medicationSafety: Avoid live vaccines unless the treating clinician specifically directs otherwise.
Do not combine biologic immunosuppressants without specialist review.
teaching: Report infection symptoms early and tell clinicians about biologic therapy before vaccines or surgery.
delegationScope: Subcutaneous administration may be within PN scope depending on policy; biologic eligibility, infection workup, and treatment holds require prescriber/RN collaboration.
examTrap: Giving the scheduled biologic to a patient with a new febrile infection because the drug is 'maintenance therapy.'
oneLinePearl: TNF blockade controls inflammation by lowering immune signaling—so infection screening and surveillance are part of the treatment.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. adalimumab prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Etanercept: TNF Inhibition and Serious-Infection Vigilance
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Etanercept is a TNF-receptor fusion protein used for inflammatory arthritis and psoriasis. The practical-nursing safety pattern is infection screening, live-vaccine avoidance, injection teaching, and rapid escalation of serious infection or neurologic/hematologic abnormalities.
recognize: Opportunistic infection risk extends beyond routine bacterial infections.
New weakness, vision changes, or sensory deficits may signal rare demyelinating complications.
priorities: Check for active infection and required baseline screening before administration.
Escalate serious infection, neurologic change, severe cytopenia symptoms, or heart-failure deterioration.
assessMonitor: Monitor infection symptoms, injection sites, neurologic status, bruising/bleeding, and heart-failure symptoms when relevant.
interventions: Use correct product-specific subcutaneous technique and storage.
medicationSafety: Live vaccines are generally avoided during therapy.
Do not assume every TNF inhibitor is interchangeable in indication or administration.
teaching: Report fever or unusual infection symptoms before taking the next dose and discuss vaccines in advance.
delegationScope: Administration may be within PN scope by policy; therapy holds and serious adverse-event evaluation require prescriber/RN input.
examTrap: Receiving a live vaccine without notifying the clinician managing TNF-inhibitor therapy.
oneLinePearl: With TNF inhibition, think infection first whenever the patient becomes unexpectedly ill.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. etanercept prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Infliximab: Infusion Reactions, TB/HBV Screening, and Delayed Hypersensitivity
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Infliximab is an IV TNF inhibitor used for several inflammatory diseases. Infusion reactions can occur during administration, while serious infection, TB/HBV reactivation, heart-failure worsening, and delayed hypersensitivity remain important between infusions.
recognize: Dyspnea, flushing, chest tightness, hypotension, urticaria, or fever during infusion can signal a reaction.
Delayed fever, rash, arthralgia, and malaise days after treatment may indicate delayed hypersensitivity.
priorities: Verify infection/TB/HBV screening and infusion orders before starting.
Stop/slow and escalate infusion reactions according to protocol and severity.
assessMonitor: Monitor vital signs, infusion symptoms, infection, liver/HBV status when indicated, and heart-failure symptoms.
interventions: Use facility biologic-infusion protocol and emergency medication readiness.
medicationSafety: Administration is infusion-protocol dependent and not universal PN authority.
Avoid live vaccines unless specifically approved.
teaching: Report both immediate infusion symptoms and delayed fever/rash/joint symptoms after leaving the infusion setting.
delegationScope: Biologic infusion administration requires state/facility competency; reaction assessment and escalation require licensed clinical judgment.
examTrap: Continuing an infliximab infusion unchanged while the patient develops chest tightness and hypotension.
oneLinePearl: Infliximab safety is both an infusion problem and an immunosuppression problem.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. infliximab prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Tofacitinib: JAK Inhibition and the Five-Part Boxed Warning
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Tofacitinib is an oral JAK inhibitor whose current boxed warning includes serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events, and thrombosis. Safe use requires infection/TB screening, CBC/liver/lipid monitoring, thrombotic/cardiovascular risk awareness, and vaccine planning.
recognize: Unilateral leg swelling, chest pain, sudden dyspnea, or neurologic deficits may indicate thrombosis/MACE.
Herpes zoster and opportunistic infections are important infection patterns.
priorities: Review infection/TB status, cardiovascular/thrombotic risk, malignancy history, CBC/liver tests, and interacting immunosuppressants.
Escalate suspected VTE/arterial event, serious infection, or severe cytopenia.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, liver tests, lipids, infection, thrombosis, cardiovascular symptoms, and treatment response.
interventions: Reinforce vaccine planning before therapy when possible and avoidance of live vaccines during treatment.
medicationSafety: May 2026 labeling retains the boxed warning for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, MACE, and thrombosis.
Combination with biologic DMARDs or potent immunosuppressants is not recommended for routine RA/PsA/AS use.
teaching: Report clot, stroke/MI, shingles, or infection symptoms urgently and keep lab-monitoring appointments.
delegationScope: Routine oral administration/monitoring may be within PN scope; boxed-warning risk selection and treatment holds require prescriber oversight.
examTrap: Choosing a JAK inhibitor as though oral administration makes it lower-risk than biologic therapy.
oneLinePearl: Tofacitinib is convenient by mouth, but its boxed risks are systemic and serious.

title: Upadacitinib: JAK-1 Therapy With Infection, MACE, Cancer, and Clot Risk
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Upadacitinib is an oral JAK inhibitor used across inflammatory diseases. Like other JAK inhibitors, safety centers serious infection/TB, malignancy, MACE, thrombosis, blood-count/liver abnormalities, and avoiding inappropriate immunosuppressant combinations.
recognize: New shingles, opportunistic infection, or persistent fever may reflect clinically important immunosuppression.
Chest pain, sudden dyspnea, limb swelling, or neurologic symptoms require urgent clot/MACE evaluation.
priorities: Review infection/TB screening, CBC/liver status, cardiovascular/thrombotic risk, and medication interactions.
Escalate serious infection, clot/MACE symptoms, or severe cytopenia.
assessMonitor: Monitor CBC, liver tests, lipids, infection, thrombotic symptoms, and treatment response.
interventions: Coordinate recommended vaccines before therapy where possible and avoid live vaccines during immunosuppression.
medicationSafety: Do not combine with other JAK inhibitors, biologic DMARDs, or potent immunosuppressants unless specialist-directed.
Extended-release tablets should be administered according to product instructions.
teaching: Seek urgent care for clot/cardiac/neurologic symptoms and report infection promptly.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within PN scope; treatment selection/holding decisions require authorized prescriber oversight.
examTrap: Continuing upadacitinib during a serious active infection without escalating to the treating clinician.
oneLinePearl: JAK inhibition is not just arthritis control—screen and watch for infection, cancer, MACE, and clots.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. upadacitinib prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Abatacept: T-Cell Costimulation Modulation and Infection/Vaccine Planning
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Abatacept reduces T-cell activation and is used for selected inflammatory arthritis. Nursing priorities are infection/TB/hepatitis risk review, vaccine planning, correct IV/subcutaneous administration, and extra respiratory vigilance in patients with COPD.
recognize: Respiratory adverse events may be more problematic in COPD.
Serious infection risk increases with overlapping immunosuppression.
priorities: Assess active infection, screening status, respiratory baseline, and concurrent biologic/JAK therapy.
Escalate serious infection, severe respiratory worsening, or hypersensitivity.
assessMonitor: Monitor infection, respiratory status in COPD, infusion/injection reactions, and treatment response.
interventions: Use route-specific administration and storage instructions.
medicationSafety: Avoid concurrent biologic DMARD combinations unless specialist-directed.
Live-vaccine timing requires clinician review.
teaching: Report infection early and discuss vaccines before receiving them.
delegationScope: Administration route/setting determines PN authority; infusion reactions and serious infection require escalation.
examTrap: Adding abatacept to another biologic because both are 'maintenance' arthritis drugs.
oneLinePearl: Abatacept lowers T-cell activation—avoid stacking immunosuppression casually.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. abatacept prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Secukinumab: IL-17 Blockade, Infection Risk, and IBD Worsening
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Secukinumab blocks IL-17A for psoriasis and selected inflammatory arthritides. Key nursing risks are serious infection, TB screening, hypersensitivity, and new or worsening inflammatory bowel disease symptoms.
recognize: Persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, or blood in stool can signal IBD onset/worsening.
Candida and other infections can occur with IL-17 blockade.
priorities: Review infection/TB status and IBD history before administration.
Escalate serious infection, anaphylaxis, or new significant GI inflammatory symptoms.
assessMonitor: Monitor infection, bowel symptoms, hypersensitivity, injection sites, and treatment response.
interventions: Teach route-specific injection technique and storage.
medicationSafety: Live vaccines are generally avoided during therapy.
Do not dismiss new bloody diarrhea as a simple medication GI effect.
teaching: Report persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, blood in stool, or infection symptoms promptly.
delegationScope: Administration may be within PN scope per policy; new IBD/infection assessment requires provider/RN collaboration.
examTrap: Treating new bloody diarrhea with an OTC antidiarrheal without considering biologic-associated IBD worsening.
oneLinePearl: IL-17 blockade: watch infection and the bowel.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. secukinumab prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Ustekinumab: IL-12/23 Blockade and Serious Infection Surveillance
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Ustekinumab targets IL-12/23 and is used in psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn disease, and ulcerative colitis. Infection/TB surveillance, malignancy awareness, hypersensitivity monitoring, and route-specific induction/maintenance administration are the main safety priorities.
recognize: Induction and maintenance routes can differ by indication.
Persistent infection or unusual skin lesions deserve evaluation rather than automatic dosing.
priorities: Verify indication, treatment phase/route, infection/TB status, and scheduled dose.
Escalate serious infection, severe hypersensitivity, or new neurologic symptoms such as PRES concern.
assessMonitor: Monitor infection, hypersensitivity, neurologic changes, skin malignancy surveillance as appropriate, and response.
interventions: Follow indication-specific IV/subcutaneous regimen and administration competency.
medicationSafety: Live vaccines require clinician review/avoidance during therapy.
Do not interchange induction and maintenance routes without verifying the regimen.
teaching: Report infection symptoms and urgent neurologic changes; keep scheduled monitoring/skin checks.
delegationScope: Route-specific biologic administration requires facility/state competency; serious adverse-event assessment requires escalation.
examTrap: Administering the maintenance injection protocol when the order is for indication-specific IV induction.
oneLinePearl: With ustekinumab, verify both immune risk and treatment phase/route.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. ustekinumab prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Rituximab: B-Cell Depletion, Infusion Reactions, HBV Reactivation, and PML
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Rituximab depletes CD20-positive B cells and is used in oncology and autoimmune disease. The highest-yield safety issues are severe infusion reactions, hepatitis B reactivation, serious infection, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, and indication-specific premedication/monitoring.
recognize: Infusion reactions can include fever, rigors, bronchospasm, hypoxia, hypotension, or anaphylaxis.
New progressive neurologic/cognitive deficits can indicate PML and require urgent evaluation.
priorities: Verify HBV screening, indication-specific premedications, infection status, and emergency readiness.
Stop/modify infusion and escalate reactions according to protocol; urgently escalate new neurologic deficits.
assessMonitor: Monitor vitals/respiratory status during infusion, HBV risk/liver status, infection, CBC as ordered, and neurologic changes.
interventions: Use infusion protocol with correct titration and emergency medications available.
medicationSafety: HBV reactivation can be severe/fatal and may occur after therapy.
Vaccines should be planned before B-cell depletion when possible; live vaccines are generally avoided.
teaching: Report neurologic changes and infection symptoms promptly even between infusions.
delegationScope: Rituximab infusion requires specialty competency and state/facility authorization; reaction and neurologic assessment require escalation.
examTrap: Treating new confusion and weakness months after rituximab as routine fatigue without considering PML.
oneLinePearl: Rituximab safety spans the infusion chair, the liver, infection risk, and the brain.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. rituximab prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Leflunomide: Hepatotoxicity, Teratogenicity, and Drug-Elimination Planning
bottomLine: Leflunomide is a conventional DMARD with major hepatic and embryo-fetal toxicity concerns and a very long-lived active metabolite. Severe toxicity or pregnancy planning may require an accelerated drug-elimination procedure rather than simply stopping tablets.
recognize: Jaundice, dark urine, marked fatigue, or severe abdominal symptoms can signal liver injury.
Because the metabolite persists, pregnancy risk can continue long after the last dose without verified elimination.
priorities: Review liver disease, pregnancy potential, CBC/liver tests, infection, and interacting hepatotoxic drugs.
Escalate pregnancy, liver injury, severe cytopenia, serious infection, or severe skin/lung reactions.
assessMonitor: Trend liver enzymes, CBC, blood pressure, infection, pregnancy-prevention status, and respiratory/skin symptoms.
interventions: Follow prescriber-directed accelerated elimination when severe toxicity or pregnancy-related clearance is required.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling requires strong attention to hepatotoxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity.
Stopping the tablet does not immediately remove the active metabolite.
teaching: Do not assume the drug is gone when tablets stop; follow the clinician's elimination/testing plan before pregnancy.
delegationScope: Routine administration/monitoring may be within PN scope; elimination procedures and reproductive-risk decisions require prescriber oversight.
examTrap: Telling a patient pregnancy is safe immediately after stopping leflunomide.
oneLinePearl: Leflunomide's metabolite lingers—sometimes you must actively wash it out.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. leflunomide prescribing information reviewed 2026
